theme: David king over all Israel; Jerusalem captured; the ark
readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 4:1-6:23. David is made king over all Israel, takes Jerusalem, and brings the ark to the city. Notice the contrast between the two attempts to move the ark.
settingTheScene: After Abner’s death, Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, is murdered by two of his own captains, and the northern tribes come to David at Hebron. He is anointed king over all Israel. He then captures the Jebusite city of Jerusalem and makes it his capital. The ark of the covenant, which had been in obscurity since 1 Samuel 7, is brought to the city, but not without tragedy.
observation: David has Ish-bosheth’s murderers executed, saying, “How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house” (4:11).
All the tribes come to Hebron and say, “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel” (5:2-3).
David takes the stronghold of Zion, “that is, the city of David” (5:7).
“And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him” (5:10).
David defeats the Philistines twice, inquiring of the LORD each time (5:17-25).
The ark is carried on a new cart, and Uzzah reaches out to steady it and dies (6:1-8).
David fears the LORD that day and leaves the ark with Obed-edom, whom God blesses (6:9-11).
David dances “before the LORD with all his might” and Michal despises him in her heart (6:14-16).
interpretation:
David’s rise to the throne over all Israel is the fulfillment of what God promised through Samuel. It is not the result of his own plotting. He has waited. When the tribes come to him, they acknowledge what God had said: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel.” The term “shepherd” is a reminder of where David came from and what a king is for.

The capture of Jerusalem makes the city “the city of David.” It will become the center of Israel’s worship and, ultimately, of the story of salvation. The narrator says plainly why David succeeded: “The LORD, the God of hosts, was with him.” His greatness is a gift.

The story of the ark in chapter 6 is a lesson on how to approach a holy God. The first attempt copies the Philistines’ method, with a new cart. The ark was to be carried by the Levites on poles. When the cart is shaken, Uzzah reaches out and is struck down. It seems harsh, and David is angry and afraid. But the lesson is that God’s holiness is not to be handled casually, even with good intentions. Good motives do not override God’s instructions.

The second attempt, three months later, is done correctly, with sacrifices and with joy. David dances before the LORD, wearing a linen ephod. He is not too proud to be undignified before God. Michal looks down on him from a window. Her scorn is the scorn of those who prefer propriety to passion. David’s answer is that he will be “even more contemptible than this” for the LORD’s sake.

The chapters show a king who inquires of God, who is awed by his holiness, and who rejoices in his presence. This is the heart of true worship: reverence and joy together.
connection: Jesus is the true presence of God in the midst of his people (John 1:14). He rode into Jerusalem while the crowds rejoiced (Matthew 21:8-9), and some wanted the disciples to be silenced (Luke 19:39-40). Hebrews 12:28 says, “Let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe.” Acts 5 shows a similar fear of God’s holiness in the early church.
application:
Ask if your worship is a mix of reverence and joy, or leans heavily in one direction.

Look at where you are doing a good thing in a way God did not instruct.

Think about whether you are afraid of looking foolish in worship, and ask God to free you.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to worship with both reverence and joy.
Confess where you have handled his word lightly.
Thank him that in Jesus he is with you.
